Use this vignette as a general guideline, not a ground truth. There is no one way to analyze genomics data. Sometimes you have to adjust your analysis based on your research question, experimental design etc. In the future you will analyze genomic data that you or other people generated. It is vital that, before any analysis, you familiarize yourself with the data set: - What is the biological question you are trying to answer? What are the hypotheses? - What is the study design and how was the experiment done (sample type, treatment, genetic knockout, disease, sample size, system, technology, are there any batches etc.)? - How was the data processed (software, genome version etc.)? - What type of data are available (raw data, count matrices, sample/cell metadata)? Instead of just copy-pasting the code, try implementing the following logic: 1. Read the vignette first. Try to understand each step. 2. Without looking at the vignette, write down the main steps of the workflow (use headers to build an outline of your document at the same time). For each step, write a short comment: What is this step for? Why is it important? Compare your answers with the vignette. It is OK if you don't remember the exact code or the name of the functions. It's more important that you understand each step conceptually. 3. After each step write down your observations. What has changed? 4. At the end of your analysis, think about and write down conclusions. It doesn't have to be an academic essay but try to state the main points and do a little bit of googling. - Are you able to answer the initial research question and confirm/deny the hypotheses? - Try to connect what is known with what you have found. The goal of this training is to help you understand the general workflow of single-cell RNA-seq analysis. Although using AI can be beneficial and speed up your analysis, it is important that you have a good understanding of topics covered in this training and you have truly mastered the skill. Only then you can use AI to help you with the analysis. It is fine to ask AI to help you with customizing a ggplot, but try not to use it for the actual analysis. If you don't know what a function does, run `?function_name` in the Console. # About the dataset We will use the `Crowell19_4vs4` dataset from the `muscData` package. It is a single-cell RNA-seq experiment of the mouse brain (prefrontal cortex) from [Crowell et al.](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-19894-4). There are 8 samples from 8 different mice: 4 were treated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a bacterial molecule that triggers an inflammatory response, and 4 with a vehicle (control). The design makes this a good example for integration and for comparing conditions: do the cells cluster by cell type or by LPS treatment, and which genes respond to LPS in each cell type? # Libraries ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(tidycomm) library(patchwork) library(Seurat) library(clustree) library(readxl) library(scuttle) library(ggridges) library(scDblFinder) library(BiocParallel) library(harmony) ``` ::: # Import data Data can be downloaded from [figshare](https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/On_the_discovery_of_population-specific_state_transitions_from_single-cell_RNA_sequencing_data/8976473). Each sample is a separate library. With the pbmc data we had only one sample, so we had to create one seurat object. Here we need to create 8 objects. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sample_metadata <- read_xlsx("data/crowell19/metadata.xlsx") ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # First we have to swap genes.tsv.gz to features.tsv.gz. otherwise seurat wont read it dirs <- list.dirs("data/crowell19", recursive = F) for (d in dirs) { old <- file.path(d, "genes.tsv.gz") new <- file.path(d, "features.tsv.gz") if (file.exists(old) && !file.exists(new)) { file.rename(old, new) } } ``` ::: ## Create seurat objects Instead of copy-pasting and adjusting code for each sample individually, we're gonna be smart about it and use a for loop to streamline the process. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # 1. It is easy with one sample. Here we have 8 samples, and we can't set one threshold for all samples, because each of them has a different distribution. We could look at individual distributions and set the thresholds manually for each sample. For 8 samples it's already a lot, so if we had 30 samples, that would be cumbersome. Instead of setting thresholds manually for each sample individually, we're gonna use some tricks to streamline the process. We will use an approach that involves MAD. **MAD** is the median absolute deviation: the median of the distances of all values from their median. It measures how spread out the values are, like the standard deviation, but it is not pulled around by extreme values. That matters here, because the low-quality cells we want to find are exactly the extreme values. A cell is marked as an outlier if its value is more than a chosen number of MADs (commonly 3) away from the median of its sample: $$\text{outlier if } |x - \text{median}(x)| > n \times \text{MAD}(x)$$ A few practical points: - **Run it per sample.** Each sample gets its own median and MAD, so the thresholds adapt to the sample. That is what makes it work for 8 samples, or 30, without setting cutoffs by hand. - **Log-transform counts and genes first.** Their distributions are skewed, so MADs work better on the log scale. - **The number of MADs is a choice.** 3 is a common default, and 5 is more permissive. Look at the plots to check that the thresholds make sense. First we will calculate percent mt for each cell. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} so <- PercentageFeatureSet(so, pattern = '^mt-', col.name = "mito.percent") # mt - because its mouse ``` ::: Let's first see how the distributions for each metric look before we do anything. I'm feeling fancy and want to make my own plots. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} multi_qc_plot <- function(seurat_obj, sample_col = 'orig.ident', metrics=c("nCount_RNA", 'nFeature_RNA', 'mito.percent') ,log_metrics = c("nCount_RNA", 'nFeature_RNA'), zoom_quantile = 0.95) { df <- seurat_obj[[]] plots <- list() for (metric in metrics) { # log10 only for the metrics listed in log_metrics (not for percentages) df$value <- df[[metric]] xlab <- metric zoom <- NULL if (metric %in% log_metrics) { df$value <- log2(df$value) xlab <- paste0("log2(", metric, ")") } else if (!is.null(zoom_quantile)) { # for metrics that are not logged, zoom in on the bulk of the cells, # so a long tail of outliers does not squish the distributions zoom <- c(min(df$value), quantile(df$value, zoom_quantile)) } plots[[metric]] <- ggplot(df, aes(x = value, y = .data[[sample_col]], fill = .data[[sample_col]])) + # ndensity scales each sample to its own peak, trim stops the density at the data range ggridges::geom_density_ridges(stat = "density", aes(height = after_stat(ndensity)), trim = TRUE) + geom_vline(xintercept = median(df$value), colour = "red") + coord_cartesian(xlim = zoom) + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Pastel2") + labs(x = xlab, y = NULL) + ggridges::theme_ridges() + theme(legend.position = "none") } return(patchwork::wrap_plots(plots)) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} multi_qc_plot(so, log_metrics = NULL ,zoom_quantile = .99) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Seurat_crowell19_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1440} ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} so[[]] %>% group_by(sample) %>% summarize( across( c(nFeature_RNA, nCount_RNA, mito.percent), list(min = min, median = median, max = max), .names = "{.col}_{.fn}" ), n_cells = n() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

What do you think might be the reasons for that? What are potential pitfalls of using MAD outliers on bimodal distributions? ::: ## Doublet detection A **doublet** is a droplet that captured two (or more) cells instead of one. Its expression profile is a mix of both cells, so it can look like a new cell type that does not exist, or it can bridge two real clusters. Doublets also tend to have more counts and more genes than single cells. The rate of doublets increases with the number of cells loaded: for 10x data it is roughly 1% for every 1,000 cells recovered, so in a sample with 5,000 cells we expect around 5%. Most tools work in a similar way: 1. Simulate artificial doublets by combining the profiles of randomly chosen pairs of cells from the same sample. 2. Place the real and the artificial cells together in a low-dimensional space (PCA). 3. Give each real cell a doublet score, based on how many of its neighbors are artificial doublets. 4. Call the cells with the highest scores doublets, using a threshold chosen by the tool. Popular tools are `scDblFinder`, `DoubletFinder`, `scds` and `Scrublet`. Things to keep in mind: - **Run it per sample (library).** Doublets can only form between cells that were in the same droplet run, so a doublet is never a mix of cells from two different samples. Running it on the merged object would be wrong. - **Run it before filtering.** Doublets are often removed by the count filters, and the tools need the full set of cells to simulate doublets from. The only filtering that should be applied before doublet detection is filtering out empty droplets, which cell ranger already does. But make sure to check the recommendations for the package that you're going to use. - **It only finds some doublets.** Doublets made of two similar cells (e.g. two neurons) look like a single cell and are hard to detect. The tools are better at doublets made of two different cell types. - **Check the result.** Look at the doublet cells on the UMAP and at their marker genes after clustering. A cluster made mostly of doublets, with markers of two cell types, can be removed. We will use `scDblFinder` `scDblFinder` doesn't work on a Seurat object; it needs a `SingleCellExperiment` object. Thankfully it is very easy to convert Seurat into SCE. We need to join the count layers before we convert Seurat to SCE. I'm gonna create a custom function to streamline the process. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} doublet_finder <- function(seurat_object, samples = "orig.ident", BPPARAM = NULL) { if (is.null(BPPARAM)) BPPARAM <- BiocParallel::SerialParam() seurat_object <- JoinLayers(seurat_object) sce <- as.SingleCellExperiment(seurat_object) # Run doublet detection (parallel if BPPARAM is a MulticoreParam/SnowParam) sce <- scDblFinder(sce = sce, clusters = TRUE, samples = samples, BPPARAM = BPPARAM) # Add doublet score and call to the Seurat metadata idx <- match(colnames(seurat_object), colnames(sce)) doublet_score <- sce$scDblFinder.score[idx] doublet <- sce$scDblFinder.class[idx] == "doublet" return(list(doublet_score = doublet_score, doublet = doublet)) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} doublets <- doublet_finder(so, samples="orig.ident", BPPARAM = BiocParallel::MulticoreParam(workers = 4)) so$doublet_score <- doublets$doublet_score so$doublet <- doublets$doublet ``` ::: This might take a while to run. Although there might be cell types that are specific to a sample or condition, it is more likely that some clusters are not driven by cell type, but by sample/library. The goal of clustering is that each cluster represents a cell type, not sample/library. That's why we often use **integration**, when we are dealing with multiple samples/libraries/batches. # Integration ## What is integration and why do we need it? Cells from different samples differ for technical reasons (library prep, sequencing depth, processing day) as well as biological ones (donor, genotype, condition). If we ignore this, cells often cluster by sample instead of by cell type, and the same cell type from two samples ends up in separate clusters. This is the classic **batch effect**. Integration is not only about technical batches. Even when there is no obvious batch, e.g. every sample was prepared separately, or all were processed together, we usually still integrate. Each sample (donor, animal, condition) is its own source of variation, and we want to line up the shared cell types across samples regardless of where the variation comes from. Here, integration means aligning shared cell populations across samples, and it is not limited to removing technical noise. **Integration** removes this sample-specific variation so that cells of the same type from different samples overlap in a shared low-dimensional space. We then cluster and annotate on the integrated embedding, which makes the clusters comparable across samples. Integration is only used for embedding, clustering and visualization. Differential expression is still done on the original (joined) expression values, not on integrated values. **Do we always need it?** No. First check whether there is a problem, e.g. a UMAP colored by sample. If samples already mix well, integration is not needed, and too aggressive integration can remove real biology (e.g. a cell type or condition effect present in only some samples). There are many integration methods, each suited for a different scenario. Sometimes we may need a harsh integration if we, for example, re-analyze public data and want to combine samples from different studies. Other times, our genetic knock-out or treatment may alter cell type composition and there might be a small subpopulation that is specific to one condition. If our integration method is too aggressive, that rare cell population might be blended with similar cell types and we ultimately lose that condition-specific rare cell type. ### General approaches - **Anchor-based / mutual nearest neighbors:** find pairs of similar cells across datasets and use them to correct one dataset towards another (Seurat CCA / RPCA, MNN, fastMNN). - **Embedding correction:** leave the expression values alone and adjust the PCA coordinates so batches overlap (Harmony). - **Probabilistic / deep learning models:** learn a latent space that is corrected for batch (scVI, scANVI). - **Reference mapping:** project new samples onto an already annotated reference instead of integrating everything together. ### Harmony We will use [Harmony](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-019-0619-0), which works on the PCA embedding. It repeatedly (1) clusters the cells softly, with a penalty for clusters dominated by a single sample, and (2) computes a cluster-specific linear correction per sample and moves the cells accordingly, until the cells are well mixed. It is fast, memory-efficient and scales to many samples. The output is a corrected embedding (`harmony`) that replaces PCA for neighbors, clustering and UMAP. Each cell in our data (or each cluster) is compared to the reference and gets the label of the most similar reference cells. Common approaches: - **Correlation-based (e.g. `SingleR`):** compares each cell's expression to reference profiles and assigns the best-matching label. It is quick and easy, with ready-made references in `celldex` (e.g. `MouseRNAseqData`, `ImmGenData`), but you can supply any annotated single-cell dataset. - **Anchor-based label transfer (Seurat `FindTransferAnchors()` + `TransferData()`):** finds matching cells between our data and an annotated Seurat reference and transfers the labels, with a prediction score for each cell. - **Pre-trained / web tools (e.g. Azimuth, MapMyCells):** map cells onto a published atlas. Things to keep in mind: - The result is only as good as the reference. It must match the species, tissue and technology, and it can only assign labels that exist in the reference. A cell type missing from the reference will be forced into the closest label. - Check the confidence scores and drop or flag low-confidence cells instead of trusting every label. It finds pairs of cells that are mutual nearest neighbors between the two datasets (the anchors), then uses those anchors to predict a label for every query cell. You are already familiar with bulk RNA-seq and the DESeq workflow. You'll see that pseudobulk is extremely easy and you use what you already know! In our DESeq tutorial we tried to compare gene expression across different conditions. That case seemed simple; we dealt with a matrix of counts gene x sample. In the single-cell world, we have another level of complexity: genes, samples/conditions and individual cells. How to deal with all of this? One of the common approaches is pseudobulk. **What is pseudobulk?** For each cell type, we **sum the raw counts** of all cells that come from the same sample. A genes × cells matrix becomes a genes × samples matrix per cell type (here 8 mice × \~17,000 genes). We then test it with the statistics developed for bulk RNA-seq (edgeR, DESeq2, limma-voom). So the only difference between bulk and pseudobulk is that in pseudobulk we have to aggregate counts from all cells across samples. The rest of the analysis is virtually the same. **Why not test cells directly?** Our experiment has 8 mice (4 vs 4), not \~24,000 replicates. Cells from the same mouse share genetics, environment and handling, so they are not independent. Treating each cell as a replicate (*pseudoreplication*) inflates confidence: methods that ignore replicate variation are biased and can report hundreds of DE genes where no biological difference exists (Squair et al. 2021). The number of "significant" genes then follows the number of cells, not the evidence (Murphy et al. 2023). Actually, we've used a method that treats each cell as a replicate in this analysis. `FindAllMarkers` does exactly that and the p-values are inflated. For marker identification it's not problematic, since we focus on top markers anyway - we do not investigate all genes, especially across conditions. **Isn't aggregation counterproductive, given single-cell resolution?**\ We lose single-cell resolution but we still keep the cell-type resolution. We aggregate within a cell type, per mouse. What we give up is cell-to-cell variability inside one cell type in one mouse, which doesn't answer the question "does LPS change expression?". What we actually gain is that summing fixes sparsity. Single-cell counts are mostly zeros. Pooling thousands of cells gives well-behaved counts for bulk methods (Squair et al. 2021). **What we lose.** Subpopulations responding differently within a cell type need finer clusters or a dedicated cell-level analysis. Pseudobulk also needs enough cells per mouse per cell type, and enough mice per group. In this dataset, clusters dominated by one mouse cannot be tested. **Is there consensus?** Pseudobulk is the usual default (Crowell et al. 2020, the paper this dataset comes from; Squair et al. 2021). Not everyone agrees: Zimmerman et al. 2021 argue it can be conservative and underpowered compared with mixed models. The robust, simple choice for a first analysis is pseudobulk. In this tutorial, we will aggregate the counts and run DGE analysis with DESeq2, but it is worth noting that this is not the only way to do it. There are other tools that have been made for single-cell pseudobulk analysis, such as [`dreamlet`](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-75680-8). ### Which cell types should be included? A pseudobulk test compares mice, so a cell type is testable only if enough mice in both conditions contribute enough cells. **Inclusion/exclusion rules (rules of thumb)** 1. At least 10 cells per cell type per mouse (arbitrary number). 2. Cell type/cluster is dominated by one replicate. This suggests a potential sampling issue when preparing libraries, making the results less reliable. It might be better to exclude that cluster. 3. Most of the replicates in each condition contribute to that cell type, e.g. 3 out of 4 mice. ::: callout-note ### Exercise 11 Prepare a table(s)/plots of "testable" cell types, based on the criteria above (use the granular annotation).
